reason: I read the Colvin text myself (Project Gutenberg 35698) and the sentence stands verbatim, comma after flower, semicolon, British favours: 'But let us open our leaves like a flower, and be passive and receptive; budding patiently under the eye of Apollo and taking hints from every noble insect that favours us with a visit--Sap will be given us for meat, and dew for drink.' The heading is XXXVII.--TO JOHN HAMILTON REYNOLDS. and the dateline [Hampstead, February 19, 1818.], so work, letter number, recipient and date are right, and the capital B is the edition's own because the preceding sentence ends at 'arrived at.' Three faults, none fatal. First, the shipped line stops mid-sentence and supplies a full stop where the edition has a dash and the sap-and-dew clause: no word is altered, so this is truncation and not minting, but the editor should know the line is two thirds of a sentence, not a whole one. Second, the Gutenberg transcription is of the Macmillan crown 8vo of 1925 (its title page reads First Edition (Globe 8vo) June 1891, reprinted 1891, 1918, 1921, 1925), so the 1891 printing named in the source is not the book that was read. Third, the evidence's 'where' is wrong about the surroundings: the sentence is not four sentences before 'I was led into these thoughts, my dear Reynolds, by the beauty of the morning' but immediately before it, and the thrush's song is verse quoted after that paragraph, not the paragraph's ending. Attribution is uncontested and absent from the misattribution list; shipped.js returns no match, no near match, Keats at 0 of 3, not banned; the tag Correspondence is the form of the work; scope, publishability and the April theme (budding patiently, passive and receptive, the eye of Apollo) all hold; the source is 116 characters, leads with the name, has no dash, and uses curly marks only.
betterCitation: John Keats, letter to John Hamilton Reynolds, 19 February 1818, Letters, XXXVII, ed. Sidney Colvin (Macmillan, 1891, repr. 1925)
